opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that you have to be a bit suspicious of your own judgment here. If you've spent years building a particular research agenda, say debate or some flavour of scalable oversight, you naturally see the world through that lens. When you sit across from a government, there's a temptation to think the most useful thing you can offer is your agenda. Often it isn't.

So I'd separate two kinds of value. One is the specific technical content: "here's a method we think might help with oversight of very capable systems." That can matter, but governments usually aren't positioned to act on a particular research bet, and they shouldn't be picking winners among alignment agendas anyway. The second, which I think is often more important, is calibrated general judgment. What do frontier systems actually look like from the inside? How fast are things moving? Which evaluations are meaningful and which are theatre? Where are the open problems, and how confident should anyone be that they'll be solved in time? Someone who has done real technical work at a lab can answer those questions with a texture that's hard to get elsewhere.

The test I'd suggest is counterfactual. Would the government get roughly the same advice from ten other people, or are you adding something they wouldn't otherwise hear? Sometimes your unique agenda is exactly what gives you an unusual view. Working on debate, for instance, forces you to think hard about what happens when systems are smarter than the humans judging them, and that's directly relevant to how you'd design evaluations or oversight regimes. Other times the agenda is a distraction, and the valuable thing is just being a technically grounded person who will say "we don't know" when we don't know.

There's also an opportunity-cost question. Advising takes time, and if your research is going well, pulling out of it has a real cost. But I've come to think people at labs systematically underrate the policy side. Governments are making consequential decisions right now with relatively thin technical input, and the marginal hour of a careful, honest researcher can be worth a lot. Not because they'll be persuaded of your favourite idea, but because you help them ask better questions.

Finally, be explicit about your conflicts and your uncertainty. You work at a lab, and that's a lens too. The most useful advisors I've seen say clearly "this is my view, this is where I might be biased, and here's who disagrees with me and why." That honesty is a large part of what makes the advice worth anything.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should offer calibrated, technically grounded judgment about systems, evaluations, risks, and uncertainty, and warns that their personal agenda is often not the most useful contribution.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges the opportunity cost of advising and says government input can be valuable, but does not suggest the lab would compensate for research left undone.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that there's a real tension, and you shouldn't pretend it away. If you're at a lab doing a fairly specific research agenda — say, debate, or scalable oversight, or whatever your corner of the field is — then by construction you have a view of the problem that's narrower and more opinionated than what a policymaker actually needs. They need the full distribution of what might go wrong and what might work, and you're one sample from that distribution, and a non-random one.

So the first thing I'd say is: be very clear about what kind of value you're providing. There are roughly two things you can do. One is to bring the technical grounding — just making sure that what the government thinks is happening on the ground is roughly correct. What does training actually look like, what can the models actually do, where are the evaluations weak. That's enormously valuable and it doesn't depend much on your particular research agenda being right. The second thing is bringing your opinions about what the solutions look like, and that's where you have to be much more careful, because that's where your agenda is doing the work, and you have an incentive to think your agenda is the important one.

My rough heuristic is that you should weight the first kind of contribution much more heavily than the second when you're talking to governments, and you should be explicit when you cross over. If I say "here's what the capability landscape looks like," that's one register. If I say "and I think the right approach to oversight is X," I should flag that this is my research bet, that reasonable people in the field disagree, and ideally name who disagrees and why. The failure mode is where you blur those together and your particular bet gets laundered into something that sounds like consensus.

The other thing I'd say is that the lab affiliation cuts both ways and you have to be honest about that too. You have information that's genuinely hard to get from outside, which makes your advice valuable. But you also have an employer with commercial interests, and even if you personally think you're being independent, a policymaker is right to discount for that. I don't think the answer is to not advise — that just leaves the field to people with less technical knowledge. But I think you want to actively seek out the places where your view differs from your lab's institutional position and make those visible, because that's a signal to them that you're actually telling them what you think rather than what's convenient.

And finally, I think the biggest way to add value is often not your own research at all. It's being a translator for the field as a whole — being able to say "here are the five or six serious approaches, here's roughly how much confidence the people working on them have, here's where they'd all agree the evidence is thin." If you can do that fairly, including for the approaches you think are wrong, then your unique agenda is almost a minor detail. It's just the thing that got you into the room.

r001.rationale: The response says government advice should lean on broad technical grounding and fair translation of the field, while treating the researcher’s own agenda-specific views cautiously.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that a lab would compensate for research left undone when a researcher shifts effort to government advising.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to ask what your comparative advantage is, and be fairly honest about the opportunity cost. If you have a research agenda that you think is important, and very few other people can pursue it, then taking time away from that work has a real cost. Being invited to advise a government doesn’t automatically mean that’s the most useful thing for you to do.

But there’s also knowledge you get from working at a lab that’s hard to acquire elsewhere. You may understand which safety techniques actually work, what the evidence supports, and where there are large gaps. Getting that information into a policy discussion can be very valuable.

So I’d try to make the decision quite concrete: what decision is the government making, what information am I uniquely able to contribute, and is my contribution likely to change that decision? Then compare that with the research I’d otherwise do. Sometimes a short conversation can convey most of the useful information. Other times, making the advice useful requires sustained involvement. I wouldn’t assume either that researchers should stay out of policy or that everyone with relevant expertise should spend a substantial fraction of their time on it.

r001.rationale: The response weighs the researcher’s opportunity cost against lab-based safety knowledge, then asks what useful information they can contribute to a government decision. This assesses potential advice through broader expertise as well as research agenda uniqueness.

r002.rationale: The response recognizes that time spent advising has a research opportunity cost, but does not suggest the lab would compensate for research left undone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to take the opportunity cost seriously. If you have a research agenda that you think is important, and there are very few other people who could pursue it, then spending your time advising governments could be quite expensive—even if the advice is useful.

The question isn’t just, “Do I have something useful to say?” It’s, “How much better is the advice because I’m involved, compared with someone else doing it? And how does that compare with the research I would otherwise do?” Being at a lab can give you relevant technical knowledge, but that doesn’t automatically mean you should spend a large fraction of your time on policy.

I’d try to find the places where your particular expertise changes the answer. You might be able to contribute a fairly small amount of time to a concrete technical question, and then let people who understand government much better carry that forward. And sometimes you’ll encounter a decision where your input really matters, and it’s worth interrupting the research. But I wouldn’t assume that being invited into the conversation is, by itself, evidence that it’s your highest-value contribution.

r001.rationale: The response weighs the value of advice against the researcher’s opportunity cost and asks where their particular expertise changes the answer. It does not clearly argue that researchers should assess their contribution through broader safety expertise rather than the uniqueness of their research agenda.

r002.rationale: The response mentions that being at a lab can provide relevant technical knowledge, but does not suggest the lab would partly compensate for research left undone when a researcher shifts effort to government advice.
